newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks close 2.31 pct lower on finance sales.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks close 2.31 pct lower on finance sales.

text.p: Thai stocks closed with pared losses on Tuesday as bargain hunters moved in to buy strong bank and finance stocks which were not suspended by officials, brokers said.
The index had dropped to as low as 634.58 by 0743 GMT after the government announced it had suspended 42 ailing finance firms in addition to 16 companies already suspended.
The composite SET index, which fell to an intraday low of 634.58 points at 0743 GMT, closed 15.35 points or 2.31 percent lower at 648.47 on 6.7 billion baht turnover.
The Thai market moved sluggishly during the morning session as investors waited for an announcement on details of the IMF rescue measures aimed at healing Thailand's ailing economy.

"Investors rushed and sold those finance firms which were suspended by authorities as soon as the announcement came out. Another announcement which came out later on the approval of measures to boost the economy didn't have much impact on the market," said Chetta Meemangkang of Prime Finance and Securities.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said Thailand had approved a series of tough measures aimed at boosting the economy with the goal of obtaining $12-$15 billion in loans from foreign countries and the IMF.

Apart from suspending 42 finance firms on Tuesday, the country also set targets of maintaining $25 billion in foreign reserves, cutting the current account deficit, controlling inflation and hiking the value added tax, Thanong said.
Thailand had previously suspended 16 ailing finance firms.
Brokers said foreigners were quite active on Tuesday as they bought some large capitalised stocks. Total net buying by foreigners on Monday amounted 348 million baht.
Stocks bought by foreigners included Bank of Ayudhya, which slipped two baht to 63.50, Electricity Generating shed 0.50 to 68.50 and Siam Cement gained two to 506.
Thai Farmers Bank topped the active list, losing one baht to 116.
